did_you_know.text: The Hebrew verb paqad does not mean only “to count”; it can also mean to take notice and act for someone. Here it describes God fulfilling His promise to Sarah.
The name Isaac is related to the Hebrew root meaning “to laugh” or “rejoice.” It recalls Abraham and Sarah’s laughter when they heard that a son would be born.
Circumcision on the eighth day is presented here as a sign of the covenant between God and Abraham’s family. The command in chapter 17 also specifies the eighth day.
In the ancient world, weaning was an important stage, when a child became less dependent on his mother. The feast may therefore have marked not just an age, but a new stage in the child’s life.
The word metzaḥeq can mean playing, laughing, or mocking, so translations understand it in different ways. It comes from the same Hebrew root as the name Isaac.
A ḥemat was a container for carrying liquids, usually a skin made from an animal hide. Such containers were especially useful in the desert, where water was essential.
A bow was important for hunting and protection, so being an archer was a skill well suited to desert life. The story presents Ishmael as someone who developed this ability.
The name Abimelech means “my father is king,” and it appears in Genesis as the name of a Philistine king. It may have been a royal name or a title used by more than one king.

In the ancient Near East, gifts, animals, and oaths could be part of ceremonies that established treaties. Here the gifts are not the covenant itself; they accompany the agreement between Abraham and Abimelech.
The name Beersheba contains a wordplay: “sheva” can recall the seven lambs, while “shevuah” means an oath, because the two sides swore to each other.

The word eshel is usually understood as the name of a tree, perhaps a desert tamarisk, though some translations understand it as a grove. A tree also suits the idea of a permanent, shaded place in the desert.
